topics.name: Adolf Hitler
topics.kicker: Nazi dictator · Started World War II in Europe, ordered the Holocaust
topics.briefing: Adolf Hitler rose from a failed 1923 coup to become Germany’s dictator, turning a defeated, struggling nation into a war machine built on hatred. As _Führer_, he tore up the Treaty of Versailles and invaded Poland in 1939 to start World War II in Europe. He ordered the Holocaust, the murder of six million Jews and millions of others, before taking his own life in 1945 as Allied armies closed in on Berlin.

trap.title: Hitler, not party or aides
trap.body: Real packets let “Adolf Hitler” score early on some tossups whose official answer is “Nazi Party,” since he led it — but once the question actually names the party, only “Nazi Party” counts. Players also confuse him with his own subordinates (Himmler, Göring, Goebbels, Hess) and with his fellow dictator Mussolini, who led Italy, not Germany.
trap.fix: If the clues describe Germany’s government, _Mein Kampf_, or being Führer and Chancellor, give his name. If the question is clearly asking for an organization (“this party,” “this corps”) or names a different person’s specific role, hold off.

topics.kicker: Italy’s Fascist dictator · Allied with Hitler through most of World War II
topics.briefing: Benito Mussolini sent his Blackshirt followers marching on Rome in 1922 and pressured the king into making him prime minister, then built Europe’s first Fascist dictatorship. As _Il Duce_ [“eel DOO-chay”], “the Leader,” he invaded Ethiopia and allied with Adolf Hitler to lead Italy through most of World War II. Italian partisans captured and executed him in April 1945, days before Hitler’s own death.

topics.name: Louis XIV
topics.kicker: France’s “Sun King” · Longest-reigning monarch, built Versailles
topics.briefing: Louis XIV became king of France at only four years old and kept the job for 72 years, still the longest confirmed reign of any monarch in European history. He expanded a royal hunting lodge into the dazzling Palace of Versailles, forced nobles to live there so he could watch them, and liked being called the “Sun King” because, like the sun, he believed everything in France revolved around him. He may never have actually said “I am the state,” but it sure sounds like him.

tossups.p: In 793, these raiders attacked the monastery of Lindisfarne [“LIN-diss-farn”] off the coast of Northumbria, a raid many historians mark as the start of their age. One of their later kings, Cnut [“kuh-NOOT”] the Great, ruled both Denmark and England at the same time.
tossups.r: This group’s power in England effectively ended at the 1066 Battle of Stamford Bridge. For 10 points, name these seafaring raiders and traders from Scandinavia.

tossups.p: A force called the Great Heathen Army, made up of these raiders and including warriors known as berserkers, invaded England in the ninth century. One of its leaders, Guthrum, eventually made peace with Alfred the Great in the Treaty of Wedmore after losing the Battle of Edington.
tossups.r: These people built fast wooden longships with shallow drafts and dragon-carved bows. For 10 points, name these seafaring raiders and traders from Scandinavia.

tossups.p: An explorer among these people, Leif Erikson, led a voyage to a land he called Vinland, reaching North America roughly five centuries before Columbus. His father, Erik the Red, had earlier founded one of this group’s settlements on Greenland.
tossups.r: Archaeologists confirmed one of their settlements at L’Anse aux Meadows [“lahnss OH meh-doh”] in Newfoundland. For 10 points, name these Scandinavian seafarers and explorers.

tossups.p: Byzantine emperors recruited some of these raiders to serve as elite palace bodyguards called the Varangian [“vuh-RAN-jee-un”] Guard. According to legend, one of their leaders, Rurik, founded a dynasty that ruled the trading city of Novgorod [“NOV-guh-rod”].
tossups.r: Others among this group paddled riverboats south to trade with, and sometimes raid, Constantinople. For 10 points, name these Scandinavian raiders and traders.

tossups.p: A Frankish king granted one of these people, a chieftain named Rollo, control of a region that became the Duchy of Normandy. Two of their kings, Gorm the Old and Harald Bluetooth, raised the carved Jelling [“YELL-ing”] Stones in Denmark.
tossups.r: Modern short-range wireless technology is named for that second king. For 10 points, name these Scandinavian raiders and settlers.

tossups.p: English kings sometimes paid these raiders tribute silver called Danegeld [“DAYN-geld”] to avoid attacks. This group also captured the English city of York and ruled it under the name Jorvik [“YOR-vik”].
tossups.r: They traveled and raided in fast longships with shallow drafts. For 10 points, name these seafaring Scandinavian raiders.

tossups.p: These raiders founded the city of Dublin in Ireland as one of their major trading settlements. Settlers of this group on Iceland founded the Althing [“AHL-thing”], often called the world’s oldest parliament.
tossups.r: They also settled Greenland and reached Newfoundland under the explorer Leif Erikson. For 10 points, name these Scandinavian explorers and raiders.

tossups.p: These people carved messages and memorials in an alphabet of symbols called runes. Some of their nobles were buried in richly furnished ships, as in the Oseberg [“OH-suh-berg”] ship burial found in Norway.
tossups.r: They sailed in longships with shallow drafts and dragon-carved bows. For 10 points, name these Scandinavian seafarers.

tossups.p: These people worshipped gods such as Odin and Thor, later recorded in a body of myths named for them. Archaeologists confirmed one of their settlements at L’Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland.
tossups.r: That settlement supports the idea that an explorer among them reached North America long before Columbus. For 10 points, name these Scandinavian raiders and explorers.

tossups.p: Slavic peoples along Russian rivers gave some of these traders the name “Rus,” possibly the origin of the name Russia. Other members of this group paddled riverboats south to trade with, and occasionally raid, Constantinople, the capital of the Byzantine Empire.
tossups.r: A leader of theirs, Rurik, is said to have founded a trading dynasty in the region. For 10 points, name these seafaring Scandinavian raiders and traders.

tossups.p: In Greenland, these people traded with, and sometimes clashed with, Inuit people they called “skraelings” [“SKRAY-lings”]. Despite a popular modern myth, these raiders almost certainly did not wear horned helmets into battle.
tossups.r: They are better known for sailing in longships with dragon-carved bows. For 10 points, name these Scandinavian seafarers and raiders.

tossups.p: This group’s long dominance in parts of England ended at the Battle of Stamford Bridge in 1066, fought just weeks before the Battle of Hastings. Two centuries earlier, one of their armies, the Great Heathen Army, had included warriors known as berserkers.
tossups.r: They built fast wooden longships with shallow drafts. For 10 points, name these seafaring Scandinavian raiders.

tossups.p: A Frankish king once granted one of these people’s chieftains, Rollo, the territory that became the Duchy of Normandy. Several of their chieftains were buried in elaborately furnished ships, including the Gokstad [“GOK-stahd”] ship found in Norway.
tossups.r: Descendants of Rollo’s settlers later crossed the English Channel and won the Battle of Hastings in 1066. For 10 points, name these Scandinavian raiders and settlers.

tossups.p: These seafarers built their longships from overlapping “clinker-built” planks around a single central keel, letting the ships sail in both open ocean and shallow rivers. Many of their ships also featured a carved dragon or serpent head on the bow.
tossups.r: They used these ships for both long-distance trade and coastal raids across medieval Europe. For 10 points, name these Scandinavian seafaring raiders and traders.

tossups.p: This group came from what are now Norway, Denmark, and Sweden, and historians generally date their age from the 793 raid on Lindisfarne to their defeat at the Battle of Stamford Bridge in 1066. Byzantine writers and Slavic peoples along Russian rivers called some of these traders the “Rus.”
tossups.r: They are popularly, but inaccurately, remembered for wearing horned helmets into battle. For 10 points, name these seafaring raiders, traders, and explorers from Scandinavia.

trap.title: Vikings, Normans, or gods?
trap.body: A tossup describing the Norse religion is really about these raiders even when it names gods like Odin or Thor — those gods are a different, wrong answer. Going the other direction, Rollo’s Viking settlers in France eventually became French-speaking Normans, so the 1066 Battle of Hastings belongs to the Normans and Anglo-Saxons, not literally to these raiders — their own English story had already ended weeks earlier at the Battle of Stamford Bridge.

topics.briefing: In 1618, Protestant nobles in Bohemia hurled Catholic officials out of a Prague castle window, igniting a war that would consume Central Europe for three decades. What began as a fight between Catholics and Protestants pulled in Sweden, Denmark, Spain, and even Catholic France, leaving the Holy Roman Empire devastated by plundering armies, famine, and disease. The Peace of Westphalia finally ended it in 1648, helping invent the modern idea that nations are sovereign.

tossups.p: This conflict began after Bohemian Protestant nobles threw royal officials out a castle window in Prague. It was sparked partly by the 1617 election of the staunchly Catholic Ferdinand II as king of Bohemia. Early on, Frederick V, the “Winter King,” was crushed at the Battle of White Mountain in 1620.
tossups.r: Sweden’s Gustavus Adolphus later entered on the Protestant side before dying at the Battle of Lützen [“LOOT-sen”]. For 10 points, name this war, fought from 1618 to 1648 and named for its length.

tossups.p: This war followed decades after the 1555 Peace of Augsburg, which had only papered over Catholic-Protestant tensions in the Holy Roman Empire. Denmark’s King Christian IV intervened on the Protestant side but was forced into the Treaty of Lübeck in 1629. Imperial generalissimo Albrecht von Wallenstein [“VAH-len-shtyne”] commanded Catholic forces until his assassination in 1634.
tossups.r: Catholic France eventually joined on the Protestant side against its Habsburg rivals. For 10 points, name this war ended by the Peace of Westphalia.

tossups.p: This war reignited after Emperor Ferdinand II’s 1629 Edict of Restitution tried to reclaim Protestant church lands. Cardinal Richelieu funneled French funding to Sweden’s war effort despite France’s own Catholic faith. Spain’s elite tercios were broken at the Battle of Rocroi [“roh-KRWAH”] in 1643.
tossups.r: It left much of Germany devastated by plundering armies, famine, and disease. For 10 points, name this seventeenth-century war that ended with the Peace of Westphalia.

tossups.p: This war’s Bohemian phase began with the defenestration of royal officials from a castle window in Prague. Gustavus Adolphus led Sweden to victory over Count Tilly at the Battle of Breitenfeld [“BRY-ten-felt”] in 1631, then died at Lützen the following year. Denmark’s Christian IV had already been forced to make peace at Lübeck.
tossups.r: It is often divided into Bohemian, Danish, Swedish, and French phases. For 10 points, name this war that devastated Central Europe from 1618 to 1648.

tossups.p: This war’s peace treaty is often credited with founding the modern idea of state sovereignty. Ferdinand II’s Edict of Restitution tried to undo Protestant land gains, reigniting the fighting in 1629. Count Tilly’s Catholic League army was defeated at Breitenfeld by Swedish forces.
tossups.r: It was fought mainly between Catholic and Protestant states within the Holy Roman Empire. For 10 points, name this war ended by the Peace of Westphalia in 1648.

tossups.p: This war began after Protestant nobles in Bohemia hurled Catholic officials out of a Prague castle window. Frederick V, called the “Winter King,” lost his throne after the Battle of White Mountain in 1620. Wallenstein, the emperor’s generalissimo, was later assassinated in 1634 amid suspicions of disloyalty.
tossups.r: It marked Europe’s last major war fought mainly over religion. For 10 points, name this war named for how long it lasted, from 1618 to 1648.

tossups.p: This war saw France, though Catholic, back the Protestant side against its Habsburg rivals, with funding arranged by Cardinal Richelieu. A French victory over Spanish tercios at Rocroi in 1643 helped bring it to a close. Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden won at Breitenfeld before dying at Lützen.
tossups.r: It followed the 1617 election of the staunchly Catholic Ferdinand II as king of Bohemia. For 10 points, name this war ended by the Peace of Westphalia.

tossups.p: This war is often divided into four phases, beginning with a Bohemian revolt after the defenestration of Prague. Denmark’s Christian IV then intervened, only to be defeated and forced into the Treaty of Lübeck. During Sweden’s phase, Gustavus Adolphus triumphed at Breitenfeld.
tossups.r: Plundering armies left much of Germany ravaged by famine and disease. For 10 points, name this war fought from 1618 to 1648.

tossups.p: This war began just two years before the brief Battle of White Mountain ended Bohemian resistance to Ferdinand II. Its underlying religious tensions dated back to the failed 1555 Peace of Augsburg. Wallenstein’s rise and eventual assassination occurred during its middle years.
tossups.r: It was fought mainly between Catholic and Protestant states in the Holy Roman Empire. For 10 points, name this war that ended with the Peace of Westphalia in 1648.

tossups.p: This war’s Swedish phase featured Gustavus Adolphus’s victory over Count Tilly at Breitenfeld in 1631. Its earlier Danish phase had ended with Christian IV’s defeat and the Treaty of Lübeck. French intervention, funded by Cardinal Richelieu, extended the fighting for years more.
tossups.r: A French victory over Spanish tercios at Rocroi in 1643 helped finally end it. For 10 points, name this war, fought from 1618 to 1648.

tossups.p: This war is often credited with establishing the modern idea of state sovereignty through the treaty that ended it. It began when Bohemian Protestant nobles threw royal officials out a castle window in Prague in 1618. Ferdinand II’s harsh Edict of Restitution reignited fighting in 1629.
tossups.r: One of the most destructive wars in European history before the twentieth century, it ravaged the Holy Roman Empire for three decades. For 10 points, name this war named for its length.

tossups.p: This war’s Bohemian phase crushed Frederick V, the so-called “Winter King,” at the Battle of White Mountain. Imperial generalissimo Wallenstein was assassinated in 1634 after a long and controversial command. Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden died winning the Battle of Lützen in 1632.
tossups.r: It ended with the Peace of Westphalia in 1648. For 10 points, name this religious and political war that began in 1618.

tossups.p: This war saw Cardinal Richelieu quietly fund Sweden’s campaigns even though his own country, France, was Catholic. The 1555 Peace of Augsburg had failed to prevent the religious tensions that caused it. Count Tilly’s Catholic League forces fell to Gustavus Adolphus at Breitenfeld.
tossups.r: France’s own entry helped defeat Spanish tercios at the Battle of Rocroi in 1643. For 10 points, name this war that devastated Germany from 1618 to 1648.

tossups.p: This war erupted after the Second Defenestration of Prague, in which Bohemian nobles threw Catholic officials from a castle window. It is often split into Bohemian, Danish, Swedish, and French phases by historians. Denmark’s Christian IV led the second of those phases before his defeat.
tossups.r: It is named simply for how long it lasted. For 10 points, name this war fought from 1618 to 1648 and ended by the Peace of Westphalia.

tossups.p: This war began over religious tensions the 1555 Peace of Augsburg had failed to resolve, worsened by the 1617 election of Ferdinand II as king of Bohemia. Gustavus Adolphus’s death at Lützen in 1632 came amid a Swedish victory. Wallenstein’s assassination followed two years later.
tossups.r: It devastated the Holy Roman Empire with plundering armies, famine, and disease for three decades. For 10 points, name this war that ended with the Peace of Westphalia.

trap.title: Which “Years’ War”?
trap.body: The Thirty Years’ War (1618–1648, Catholics vs. Protestants in the Holy Roman Empire) is easy to confuse with the Hundred Years’ War (1337–1453, England vs. France), since both are named for how long they lasted. It also gets mixed up with the English Civil War, a religious and political conflict happening in England around the same years.
trap.fix: Check the dates and the place: 1618–1648 in the Holy Roman Empire (mostly Germany) means the Thirty Years’ War; 1337–1453 between England and France means the Hundred Years’ War; Charles I and Oliver Cromwell mean the English Civil War.

topics.name: Battle of Stalingrad
topics.kicker: WWII’s Eastern Front turning point · Soviets encircled a trapped German army
topics.briefing: In the summer of 1942, German forces pushed deep into southern Russia, aiming to seize oil fields in the Caucasus and capture a city on the Volga River that bore the Soviet leader’s name. Street-by-street fighting dragged on for months around landmarks like Pavlov’s House and the hill of Mamayev Kurgan, until a massive Soviet counterattack, Operation Uranus, encircled the German Sixth Army. Its surrender in February 1943 marked the turning point of World War II’s Eastern Front.

tossups.p: An anti-aircraft regiment staffed largely by young women helped defend this battle’s namesake city. Fighting here earned the grim nickname “Rat War” from German soldiers because of brutal house-to-house combat. A famous photograph from the ruins shows a fountain statue of children dancing in a circle, still standing amid the wreckage.
tossups.r: Operation Uranus, launched in November 1942, encircled the trapped German Sixth Army here. For 10 points, name this World War II battle fought in a city on the Volga River.

tossups.p: Soviet sniper Vasily Zaytsev [“ZYT-sef”] became famous for his skill during this battle. It grew out of Germany’s Case Blue offensive, which aimed to seize oil fields in the Caucasus. A small Soviet garrison held out for about two months inside a ruined apartment block called Pavlov’s House.
tossups.r: German commander Friedrich Paulus was promoted to field marshal just before becoming the first German field marshal ever to surrender. For 10 points, name this battle, the turning point of the Eastern Front.

tossups.p: Fighting in this battle reached the floor of a tractor factory that had been turning out T-34 tanks. Control of the hilltop Mamayev Kurgan [“mah-MY-yev koor-GAHN”] changed hands repeatedly, and a giant statue called The Motherland Calls stands there today. Soviet generals Georgy Zhukov and Aleksandr Vasilevsky [“vah-see-LEV-skee”] planned the encirclement that trapped the German attackers.
tossups.r: It began under the shadow of Stalin’s Order No. 227, which threatened to punish any soldier who retreated. For 10 points, name this World War II battle fought in southern Russia.

tossups.p: This battle included a two-month stand by a small Soviet garrison inside a ruined apartment block called Pavlov’s House. It grew out of Germany’s Case Blue offensive, which had aimed at Caucasus oil fields. Operation Uranus, launched in November 1942, encircled the German Sixth Army trapped inside the city.

Vasily Zaytsev’s sniping made him famous during it. Stalin’s Order No. 227 had forbidden retreat without permission as it began.

trap.title: The Battle, or the Man?
trap.body: Because the city of Stalingrad was named for Joseph Stalin, this battle shares many clues with him: the Sixth Army, Order No. 227, and the Eastern Front. It is also easy to mix up with Operation Barbarossa (the 1941 invasion that opened the Eastern Front) and the Battle of Kursk (a later tank battle on the same front).
trap.fix: “Name this battle” or “this siege” wants Stalingrad; “name this leader” wants Stalin himself. Barbarossa was the 1941 invasion; Kursk came half a year later and featured the largest tank battle in history, not Pavlov’s House or Operation Uranus.
trap.line: Real answer line: Battle of Stalingrad (accept Siege of Stalingrad)

topics.name: Berlin Wall
topics.kicker: Cold War barrier through Berlin · Fell in 1989
topics.briefing: East Germany built the Berlin Wall overnight in August 1961 to stop its own people from fleeing to the West, ringing West Berlin with concrete, barbed wire, and guard towers. For 28 years it split friends, families, and one city in half, until crowds poured through its suddenly opened gates on November 9, 1989. Today, painted fragments and a double line of cobblestones in the pavement are almost all that’s left.

sample.note: the 6 real QBReader tossups that came up for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked; 2 of them primarily wanted the city “Berlin,” accepting “Berlin Wall” as an alternate)

tossups.p: After World War II split a German capital into four occupying zones, the three Western ones merged into a democratic island deep inside Communist territory. To stop the “Brain Drain” of skilled workers fleeing to that island, authorities sealed its border overnight in August 1961, first with barbed wire and then with concrete.
tossups.r: This barrier’s most famous crossing point was Checkpoint Charlie, near where a young bricklayer named Peter Fechter was shot in 1962 and left in the “death strip.” For 10 points, name this structure that divided a German capital into East and West until 1989.

tossups.p: Shortly before this barrier went up, East Germany was losing more than a thousand people a day to the West, many of them skilled workers, a “Brain Drain” its builders hoped to stop. Its planners even gave it a propaganda name, the “antifascist protective rampart,” and raised it almost overnight with barbed wire that was later replaced by concrete slabs.
tossups.r: President Ronald Reagan later stood at the Brandenburg Gate and urged Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev [“GOR-buh-chawf”] to tear it down. For 10 points, name this Cold War structure that split a divided German city for 28 years.

tossups.p: In 1986, artist Keith Haring painted a long mural of linked human figures on this structure’s western side. A later painting, Dmitri Vrubel’s “My God, Help Me to Survive This Deadly Love,” shows East German leader Erich Honecker [“HOH-neck-er”] and Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev [“BREZH-neff”] kissing in greeting.
tossups.r: Vrubel’s mural is part of the East Side Gallery, the longest surviving section of this barrier. For 10 points, name this structure whose fall in 1989 is now celebrated with murals and museums in a reunified German capital.

tossups.p: On the night of November 9, 1989, an East German spokesman named Günter Schabowski [“SHAH-boff-skee”] mistakenly announced at a press conference that a new travel policy would start “immediately.” Crowds raced to crossing points and overwhelmed confused guards, who eventually opened the gates without orders from above.
tossups.r: Demolition of this barrier continued through 1990, the same year Germany formally reunified. For 10 points, name this Cold War structure whose sudden fall that night is now remembered every November 9th.

tossups.p: This structure’s “death strip” no-man’s-land included raked sand to reveal footprints, floodlights, guard dogs, and spike strips nicknamed “Stalin’s carpet.” Watchtowers overlooked the whole stretch, and guards there had standing shoot-to-kill orders for anyone trying to cross.
tossups.r: A bricklayer named Peter Fechter died in this zone in 1962 after being shot while trying to escape. For 10 points, name this heavily guarded Cold War barrier that divided a German capital for 28 years.

tossups.p: More than a decade before this structure existed, a Soviet blockade of the city it would later divide was broken by an airlift, as American and British planes flew in supplies for nearly a year. One pilot, Gail Halvorsen, became known as the “Candy Bomber” for dropping treats to children below.
tossups.r: That 1948–49 crisis previewed the divide that this barrier made permanent in 1961. For 10 points, name this Cold War structure that split a German capital until 1989.

tossups.p: The Western Allies named three of their checkpoints using the NATO alphabet: Alpha, Bravo, and Charlie. The last of those became the main crossing for foreigners and Allied personnel, and the site of a tense tank standoff between American and Soviet forces in October 1961.
tossups.r: That crossing, Checkpoint Charlie, became the best-known landmark of this barrier. For 10 points, name this Cold War structure, demolished after 1989, that divided a German capital into two halves.

tossups.p: At least 5,000 people are estimated to have escaped across this barrier by tunneling underneath it, leaping from windows of border buildings, or hiding in secret compartments built into cars. At least 140 people died at this barrier over nearly three decades.
tossups.r: Those numbers made this one of the deadliest borders of the Cold War. For 10 points, name this heavily guarded structure that divided a German capital from 1961 to 1989.

tossups.p: In a 1987 speech at the Brandenburg Gate, President Ronald Reagan directly challenged Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev to tear down this structure if he truly wanted peace and openness. Two years later, crowds streamed through its opened gates and began chipping it apart with hammers and chisels.
tossups.r: Chunks of this barrier were later sold as souvenirs around the world. For 10 points, name this Cold War structure whose fall in 1989 helped end the division of Germany.

tossups.p: Builders eventually replaced an initial barbed-wire fence with concrete slabs about 12 feet tall, topped with smooth pipe meant to stop anyone from climbing over. Rather than running only through downtown, it stretched about 96 miles to encircle an entire isolated half of a city.
tossups.r: That encircled half was West Berlin, an island of democracy deep inside Communist East Germany. For 10 points, name this Cold War barrier that surrounded it until 1989.

tossups.p: Because builders raised this barrier overnight on a Sunday with almost no warning, some residents woke up on August 13, 1961, suddenly unable to reach relatives, friends, or jobs across town. Most train and subway links between the two sides were cut the same day.
tossups.r: Many families remained separated by this barrier for the better part of three decades. For 10 points, name this Cold War structure that abruptly divided a German capital starting in 1961.

tossups.p: Several of a divided city’s subway and commuter-rail lines briefly ran beneath its eastern half, so trains from the western side passed without stopping through sealed “ghost stations.” Guards even patrolled some of those unused platforms underground.
tossups.r: Those eerie stations reopened only after this barrier came down. For 10 points, name this Cold War structure that forced a divided city’s transit system to work around it from 1961 to 1989.

tossups.p: Today, a double row of cobblestones set into a reunified capital’s streets traces the old path of this vanished structure. Museums, preserved guard towers, and an open-air mural gallery along its longest surviving stretch now mark where it once stood.
tossups.r: That gallery takes its name from the eastern side it once faced. For 10 points, name this Cold War structure, demolished after 1989, that once divided a German capital in two.

tossups.p: Soviet premier Nikita Khrushchev [“KROOSH-chef”] had demanded Western withdrawal from a divided city for years before this structure finally sealed its border by surprise. Western leaders, caught off guard, chose not to intervene militarily, accepting the new barrier rather than risk war.
tossups.r: Its construction hardened a line that had already split the city since the end of World War II. For 10 points, name this Cold War structure that physically divided a German capital from 1961 to 1989.

tossups.p: When this structure finally fell, commentators around the world called it the symbolic end of the Cold War, since it had stood for decades as the clearest physical line between NATO and Soviet-backed Europe. Celebrations at the site were broadcast live to a global audience that same night.
tossups.r: Within a year of its fall, East and West Germany formally reunified as one country. For 10 points, name this Cold War structure whose collapse in November 1989 is remembered as a turning point in world history.

trap.title: Wall, Airlift, or Iron Curtain?
trap.body: Several different Cold War “Berlin” answers get mixed up. The Berlin Airlift (1948–49) was a supply operation that happened 13 years before this wall even existed, and the “Iron Curtain” was Winston Churchill’s broader term for the whole border between Communist and Western Europe, not this one city’s wall. Some real tossups also want just “Berlin” the city rather than this specific structure, especially when the clues describe the divided city as a whole.
trap.fix: Brain Drain, Checkpoint Charlie, barbed wire and concrete, and the 1989 fall mean this wall specifically. Candy-dropping pilots and a 1948 blockade mean the Airlift. A line running through all of Eastern Europe, not just one city, means the Iron Curtain.
trap.line: Real answer lines: Berlin Wall [or Berliner Mauer] and, on some sets, Berlin [accept Berlin Wall]
